title: The secret lifecycle: inventory, ownership and rotation
summary: How the parts of this lesson fit together.

steps.n: Passwords, API keys, tokens, private keys, signing keys, database credentials, webhook URLs with tokens and cloud access keys are all secrets.
For each secret record what it protects, who owns it, where it is stored, who can read it and when it was last changed.
Rank secrets by what an attacker could do with them.
Scheduled rotation limits how long a stolen secret works.
Write the leak plan before it is needed: who is called, how the secret is revoked, how the new one is deployed, how to check the access logs for misuse and how to tell affected people.
Confirm the outcome with a metric, a query or a test, and write down what changed so the next person can repeat it.

title: Failure and recovery: A key that nobody dared to rotate
summary: A realistic failure and the way back.

steps.n: The system works and the team relies on it, so nobody is watching this particular risk closely.
A cloud access key was found in a public repository and nobody knew which systems used it.
An operator runs a command such as: aws iam list-access-keys --user-name deploy-bot --query "AccessKeyMetadata[].[AccessKeyId,CreateDate,Status]"
The key was over four years old, had broad permissions and had no recorded owner.
The team feared that disabling it would break production, so it stayed active for two days while they searched.
The team closes the gap: avoid this mistake: No owner for a secret.
The incident is reviewed for system and process causes and the runbook is updated so the next responder finds the answer faster.

title: Finding and stopping leaks in code, CI and images
summary: How the parts of this lesson fit together.

steps.n: Typical leaks are a key in a configuration file, a token printed in a build log, a credentials file copied into an image layer, a secret pasted into a ticket and an environment dump in a crash report.
A pre commit hook catches many mistakes before they leave a laptop, but hooks can be skipped.
Scanning only the current files misses secrets removed in later commits.
Mask secrets in CI output and never echo them.
Assume any exposed secret is compromised.
Confirm the outcome with a metric, a query or a test, and write down what changed so the next person can repeat it.

title: Failure and recovery: A token in a build log
summary: A realistic failure and the way back.

steps.n: The system works and the team relies on it, so nobody is watching this particular risk closely.
A token for the package registry appeared in a public build log after a debug flag was turned on.
An operator runs a command such as: grep -n "npm_" build-4821.log | head -2
A developer had enabled verbose output while debugging, and the tool printed its configuration, including the token.
The team revoked the token within minutes, checked the registry audit log for downloads and publishes, deleted the log and issued a scoped token stored as a masked variable.
The team closes the gap: avoid this mistake: Relying only on a pre commit hook.
The incident is reviewed for system and process causes and the runbook is updated so the next responder finds the answer faster.

title: Delivering secrets to Kubernetes workloads
summary: How the parts of this lesson fit together.

steps.n: A Secret is base64 encoded data stored in etcd.
The operator reads values from an external store such as a cloud secret manager or Vault and creates native Secrets in the cluster.
The driver mounts secrets from an external store as files in the pod when it starts, and can optionally create a Secret too.
SOPS encrypts the values in a file with a key from a cloud key service or an age key, so the file can be committed safely and decrypted by the deployment tool.
Environment variables are simple but appear in process listings, crash dumps and child processes, and do not change without a restart.
Confirm the outcome with a metric, a query or a test, and write down what changed so the next person can repeat it.

title: Failure and recovery: The rotation that the pods never saw
summary: A realistic failure and the way back.

steps.n: The system works and the team relies on it, so nobody is watching this particular risk closely.
A database password was rotated and the application kept failing until every pod was restarted.
An operator runs a command such as: kubectl get externalsecret db-creds -n shop -o jsonpath="{.status.refreshTime}"

The operator refreshed the Secret on time, but the application read the password from an environment variable at start, so running pods kept the old value and failed after the old password was revoked.
The team mounted the value as a file, made the application re read it on failure and added a rolling restart trigger when the Secret changed.
The team closes the gap: avoid this mistake: Believing base64 means encrypted.
The incident is reviewed for system and process causes and the runbook is updated so the next responder finds the answer faster.

title: Certificate inventory, expiry monitoring and revocation
summary: How the parts of this lesson fit together.

steps.n: Public sites, internal services, load balancers, mail servers, VPN gateways, databases, client certificates, code signing certificates and certificates embedded in appliances.

Combine several views: certificate transparency logs for public names, cloud certificate manager listings, Kubernetes certificate objects, scans of your address ranges for TLS endpoints and the issuance logs of your internal CA.
Probe the real endpoint and read the certificate that clients see, because the one in a store may not be the one deployed.
A certificate authority can revoke a certificate and publish that in a revocation list or answer status queries with OCSP.
Certificates valid for days or weeks limit the damage from a stolen key and force automation to work.
Confirm the outcome with a metric, a query or a test, and write down what changed so the next person can repeat it.

title: Failure and recovery: The certificate on the forgotten gateway
summary: A realistic failure and the way back.

steps.n: The system works and the team relies on it, so nobody is watching this particular risk closely.
A partner integration failed at night because a certificate on an old gateway expired.
An operator runs a command such as: echo | openssl s_client -connect gw.example.com:443 -servername gw.example.com 2>/dev/null | openssl x509 -noo
The gateway was set up three years earlier by a team that had since moved, and its certificate was renewed by hand each year.
It was not in any inventory and no alert covered it.
The team closes the gap: avoid this mistake: Trusting a store listing instead of the live endpoint.
The incident is reviewed for system and process causes and the runbook is updated so the next responder finds the answer faster.

title: Operating cert-manager: issuers, ACME and failures
summary: How the parts of this lesson fit together.

steps.n: You define an Issuer or ClusterIssuer that describes the authority, and a Certificate that asks for names.
HTTP-01 proves control by serving a token over port 80, so it needs the name to be reachable from the internet and cannot issue wildcards.
By default cert-manager renews when about a third of the lifetime remains, and updates the Secret in place.
Public authorities limit how many certificates can be requested for a name in a period.
Run describe on the Certificate, then on its CertificateRequest, Order and Challenge, reading the events at each level.
Confirm the outcome with a metric, a query or a test, and write down what changed so the next person can repeat it.

title: Failure and recovery: A certificate that stayed pending for a day
summary: A realistic failure and the way back.

steps.n: The system works and the team relies on it, so nobody is watching this particular risk closely.
A new service had no certificate after the deployment and the ingress served a default one.
An operator runs a command such as: kubectl describe challenge -n shop | grep -E "State|Reason"
The ingress rule for the service forced a redirect and a rewrite that sent the challenge path to the application, which returned 404.
The team allowed the challenge path through, deleted the failed Challenge so that it retried, and the certificate became ready in a minute.
The team closes the gap: avoid this mistake: Using the production endpoint while testing.
The incident is reviewed for system and process causes and the runbook is updated so the next responder finds the answer faster.

title: Workload identity, SPIFFE and key management
summary: How the parts of this lesson fit together.

steps.n: A workload presents a signed token that says who it is and where it runs, and the receiving system maps that to permissions.
A pipeline or a pod receives a short lived signed token from its platform.
SPIFFE defines a standard identity name for a workload and a format for proving it, usually an X.509 certificate or a signed token.
A key management service stores master keys in hardware backed storage and never reveals them.
Rotate master keys on a schedule, which usually keeps old versions for decrypting existing data.
Confirm the outcome with a metric, a query or a test, and write down what changed so the next person can repeat it.

title: Failure and recovery: A role that any repository could assume
summary: A realistic failure and the way back.

steps.n: The system works and the team relies on it, so nobody is watching this particular risk closely.
A federation trust accepted tokens from any repository in the organisation.
An operator runs a command such as: aws iam get-role --role-name deploy-prod --query "Role.AssumeRolePolicyDocument.Statement[0].Condition"
The role trusted every repository in the organisation, so a test repository with weak review could obtain production deploy rights.
A review found it before misuse.
The team closes the gap: avoid this mistake: Wildcard subjects in a federation trust.
The incident is reviewed for system and process causes and the runbook is updated so the next responder finds the answer faster.
